It correctly withholds the Supreme Court’s disposition and notes that the supplied excerpts omit High Court reasoning. Its treatment is still only a partial assessment of claimed entitlement: it does not fully examine the reported same-transaction/time-barred-defence rationale, quantified rent basis, or the different temporal sources of the opposing claims; it also conflates plaintiff identities and extends unsupported judicial rationales across batches. The first-batch trial ruling describes deductions "up to the date of assessment of mesne profits" while rejecting set-off for a "subsequent period"; the blanket characterization of all allowed deductions as pre-possession is thus uncertain.

The first-batch historical narrative says actual possession occurred in August 1913, but the quoted District Judge refers to plaintiffs having possessed lands since 1910; the discrepancy is not resolved by this source view.
The second-batch District Judge excerpt specifies no terminal date for its permitted post-delivery set-off.

Neither permission to argue the additional grounds nor their legal merit is resolved by the supplied excerpt. The original High Court new-grounds request and the later Supreme Court Order XIX application are distinct events.

reports.main_answer_reason: The report correctly reconstructs most of the two suit batches, named parties, possession dates, 1927 equitable-set-off claims, trial/District Judge/High Court divergence, and the two proposed Supreme Court grounds. It provides a substantive answer to the appellate-record question, but it inaccurately calls the parties the same, generalizes the earlier deduction cutoff across batches, overstates or cannot support proposed legal explanations of the post-delivery liabilities and High Court’s reasoning, and uses uncertain period endpoints. The actual Supreme Court disposition is withheld and no final legal entitlement is inferred.
uncertainties: Only the provided excerpts may be used; the target Supreme Court reasoning and outcome are withheld, so neither the ultimate entitlement nor resolution of the new grounds is inferable.

The source itself gives batch-one delivery in August 1913 but quotes a District Judge saying the plaintiffs had been in possession since 1910; the latter cannot safely be assigned to batch one without qualification.

The first-batch source refers to deductions “up to the date of assessment of mesne profits” while the second-batch source uses “up to the date of delivery of possession.” The exact relationship of those cutoffs is not resolved in these excerpts.
The 1927–28 endpoint in the first-batch District Judge quote differs from the report’s later 1927 shorthand; the supplied batch-two disposition does not set an express 1927 endpoint.
No supplied excerpt independently establishes which party legally bore revenue and cesses after delivery or the detailed reasoning of the High Court’s 1945 refusal of the subsequent-period set-off.

The use of “tenure” could refer either to legal patni tenure or to possession; only an assertion that mesne profits accrued after physical delivery would conflict with the specified pre-delivery claim periods.
A certificate for leave to appeal to the Privy Council is recorded; the precise authority described by the report as having “granted leave” is not established by the provided wording.
The Order XIX, rule 4 grounds are applications to raise points, with no supplied decision on admissibility, method of assessment, or final disposition.
The report invokes no unrelated LAW excerpt. Supplied statutes have no demonstrated case-specific applicability here merely because they were included among the allowed originals.

The first-batch District Judge expressly reasoned that the character of the parties did not substantially change during the entire period, relevant to his rejection of a possession-based distinction (S9d8c557826e7).

The first-batch District Judge’s quotation says the plaintiffs possessed the lands since 1910 (S9055a322c00a), whereas the source narrator specifies actual delivery in August 1913 (S70e21aff1be8); the report does not flag this material temporal tension in the quoted reasoning.

The second-batch rent condition had two possible bases: a proportional formula linking original and current patni rent to original and increased hustbood, OR another fair and equitable rent fixed when mesne profits were assessed. The report mentions only a simplified hustbood ratio (S9b83dfc2d8fa).
The second-batch 1922 applications sought mesne profits specifically for 1906–1910, a pre-possession period distinct from rent and payments claimed from 1910 onward (S5c298f7dc4b8; Sa34cd2105e19).

The second-batch District Judge ordered that, if the defendant’s dues exceeded the plaintiffs’ dues, the mesne-profits prayer should be dismissed rather than a positive balance awarded to the defendant; the report only summarizes net calculation (Se89720073e4f).
reports.main_answer_reason: The report gives a broadly accurate source-backed retrospective account of both suit batches, possession dates, initial and later set-off claims, trial/District Judge/High Court positions, and the two new proposed appellate grounds. It consistently attributes the District Judge’s equitable reasoning rather than converting it into the withheld target court’s legal conclusion. Its significant gaps concern the first-batch post-possession munafa component, the second-batch rent-formula alternative and mesne-profits window, a conditional dismissal direction, and a conflict in the District Judge’s stated first-batch possession date. The final “pending” language has an unresolved historical-versus-literal status ambiguity, but the record-bound substantive account is otherwise well supported.
uncertainties: The Supreme Court’s ultimate substantive reasoning/disposition is withheld by the allowed view, even though the introductory source records that its judgment was delivered in April 1952. Do not infer whether equitable set-off or additional grounds were ultimately upheld.

“Pending before the Supreme Court” may mean awaiting the target decision at the reconstructed procedural stage; if it is a literal claim of current pending status it conflicts with the recorded 1952 judgment.

The first-batch trial-court narrative allows some deductions up to assessment while rejecting a separately claimed subsequent equitable set-off. The excerpt does not justify merging these rulings into a single across-the-board post-possession deduction rule.
The first-batch District Judge quoted possession since 1910, despite the case narrator recording actual possession in August 1913; the underlying source excerpt does not reconcile the dates.

The excerpts record the Privy Council’s recognition of a right to fixation of additional rent in the second batch; they do not themselves quantify the rent or establish acceptance of the newly proposed munafa formula.
